Illustration by Fresh Idea

Full manuscript in two months. That was the goal. I was on vacation in Mexico, no less, when I checked my email and saw the opportunity. It was mid-June and the conference was happening near the city of Oaxaca. The invitation was from a publisher looking for innovative short stories, exactly what I wanted to work on while relaxing on the beach and enjoying the sun. I felt my ego swelling as I imagined myself being among the top contenders, sharing my story with literary experts and fellow writers.

But something unexpected happened once I returned home. My ego, now more than just a feeling, became my greatest adversary. Each time I sat down to write, I found myself second-guessing every sentence, each character's motivation, and the overall flow of the narrative. I had become so critical that I couldn’t write a single page without tearing it apart or adding unnecessary complexity to the plot, just to prove how clever I could be.

The problem lay in my mindset. While ambition is often necessary for great writing, an inflated sense of self can paralyze even the most talented writers. The urge to be original and stand out led me to overthink and overcomplicate. My initial excitement was replaced by anxiety, and the idea of submission felt like a leap into the unknown.

I tried to shake off this newfound blockage by setting realistic goals for daily writing, but even those small wins were overshadowed by the looming fear of failure. Every word felt like a risk, and I found myself stuck in a loop of revision and doubt.

It took stepping away from the manuscript completely for a few days to realize that my approach needed a radical shift. I began reading the works of other writers whose styles resonated with me. Instead of focusing on uniqueness, I decided to focus on authenticity. I reminded myself that no story is entirely new; rather, it’s the telling that makes it special.

This change in perspective helped liberate my ego.

So, as I sit here reflecting on my own struggles, I’d like to share three keys to manifesting a long-term love life immediately.

One of the first lessons I learned from Charice and Johann is the importance of vulnerability and openness in communication. Too often, I’ve hidden behind a wall of silence or sarcasm, pretending that I’m okay when I’m not, and avoiding difficult conversations that could have prevented misunderstandings or conflicts. Vulnerability requires us to be honest about our feelings and to trust that our partner will respond with empathy and understanding.

When I finally decided to let down my guard and talk openly with my partners, I was surprised to find that they were just as willing to share their deepest thoughts and fears.
